details.reason: The evidence states that AdamPM “does not pool the first moment and follows Adam’s element-wise update,” initializes and updates an m×n first-moment matrix, and stores mn first-moment elements. It also states that AdamPM pools/compresses only the second moment by grouping s adjacent entries within rows or columns and storing a compressed m×q second-moment state.

The evidence directly states that AdamPM averages squared gradients within each group before applying the EMA, maintains only the compressed second-moment state persistently, temporarily broadcasts each group statistic for the parameter update, and stores mn first-moment plus mn/s second-moment elements, totaling mn(1 + 1/s), compared with 2mn for Adam.

The evidence states that LIS uses interpretable SAE feature-guided coverage selection, defines safety-related features as those activated more often on safety data than general data, and says the general dataset used for identification is Alpaca.

The figure shows harmful prompts and over-refusal prompts both going through 'Word-avg greedy coverage' of the safety feature set, where each step picks the highest-scoring prompt and adds newly covered features, repeated until the feature set is covered.

The text says 1,200 samples are selected from TRIDENT-Edge as LIS-Safety and 1,200 from OR-Bench-80K as seeds for LIS-Over-Refusal. The figure shows selected harmful prompts keep their safe responses, and over-refusal seeds go into synthesis.

The figure depicts the over-refusal seeds entering a multi-agent adversarial synthesis loop: Generator rewrites into a harder prompt, Guard checks if it is flagged unsafe, Judge checks if it is actually harmless, feedback/retry occurs on failures, and Writer produces a helpful answer.

The evidence says MeltKV jointly co-designs index bit-width/precision assignment with memory-aligned storage layout, categorizes channel/key groups into high, medium, and low precision, and stores the resulting indices compactly in standard uint8/uint16 formats, eliminating redundant bits.

Figure 4 explicitly shows the power-of-two method with n_Low=6 and n_High=10 packed as 6bit+10bit into a uint16, and n_Mid=8 stored as an 8bit field in uint8. Text also states medium precision is restricted to 8 bits and low/high are packed into 16 bits.

For non-power-of-two settings, the text states low and medium indices are extended to 7 and 9 bits and packed into uint16. It also states high-variance groups are partitioned into two c/2 segments with n=8 and encoded as two uint8 indices; the figure depicts the same layout.

The evidence distinguishes key and value storage: the proposed variable-bit packing scheme stores key indices in uint8/uint16 formats, while value indices use a fixed uint8 scale. It explicitly says that only for the effective 3-bit configuration of values, n=6 is selected with two zero-bit paddings.
The table's Dataset row for the entire LLMFineTuningBench lists ✓[%] as 36.8, where ✓ is defined as the ratio of jobs that ran successfully.
The OPT-1.3B block in Table 1 lists AVG scores of 66.7 for StructZO, 63.0 for MeZO, and 67.2 for FO-Adam.
Table 2 reports GLUE accuracy averages: for GPT-2-XL, LOREN Avg. is 71.4 and ENGINE Avg. is 73.4 with ∆vs LOREN +2.0; for OPT-2.7B, LOREN Avg. is 70.8 and ENGINE Avg. is 72.9 with ∆vs LOREN +2.1.

The evidence for paper-003 shows tables/plots comparing against both MeZO and LOZO. The paper-007 text explicitly says StructZO compares with ZO baselines including MeZO and LOZO. The paper-008 text says its OPT-13B/OPT-30B comparisons use/keep MeZO and LOZO rows. Thus all three cited works compare against both MeZO and LOZO, making them shared baselines.

The ENGINE figure/table shows, under SuperGLUE BF16 for OPT-13B, MeZO has RTE accuracy 59.0. The controlled OPT comparison table shows MeZO on OPT-13B RTE as 60.4 ± 1.5. Thus the cited evidence supports the stated numerical difference.

The ENGINE setup text states that all baselines are independently reproduced under LOREN’s setup and that mean accuracy over five seeds is reported. The controlled comparison table states it uses fixed report-seed hyperparameters and symmetric development-loss checkpoint selection, and that OPT-13B results are mean ± sd over three seeds. Thus the evidence supports the described protocol differences.

The evidence states that MeltKV is a KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving, reduces memory usage, uses memory-aligned variable-bit index packing to eliminate redundant bits, and uses head-wise codebook sharing to reduce codebook size.

The evidence describes SMELL as a federated long-context LLM fine-tuning framework addressing excessive activation memory on resource-constrained devices, not an inference KV-cache method. It identifies LSFA as a mechanism enabling memory-efficient local adaptation, and the reported context-length sweep says savings relative to FwdLLM+LoRA increase with context length, indicating sparse forward computation becomes more valuable as input grows.

The evidence states that AdamPM is a minimally modified Adam variant that pools/groups adjacent second-moment entries and shares one statistic/mean within each group; it also states grouping is along the row or column dimension and that group size s reduces second-moment memory to 1/s of the original.

The evidence describes StructZO as a structured zeroth-order framework that improves forward-only optimization, and states it avoids backpropagation, backward activation storage, and Adam optimizer states. It also states its main extra memory is an informative basis P and that, with resampling, perturbations and reduced-space estimates are regenerated from random seeds rather than storing all q query directions.

The AdamPM evidence supports that it reduces optimizer-state memory by pooling the second-moment state, i.e. compressing part of Adam’s state. The StructZO evidence states it avoids backpropagation, backward activation storage, and Adam optimizer states, and discusses it in the context of ZO baselines/multi-query estimation, supporting that it removes those memory costs via a different optimization approach.
Panel (c) lists GPU model failure ratios as L40S 69%, A100 SXM 63%, A100 PCIe 58%, and H100 PCIe 49%; thus H100-PCIe has the lowest shown failure ratio, at 49%.

The figure's GPU Memory Comparison chart includes OPT-13B and shows a bracket comparing FO-Adam with StructZO labeled 11.2×. This supports that StructZO uses 11.2× less GPU memory than FO-Adam on OPT-13B.

The 1-bit panel shows n=8 and mixed both using about 0.25 GB, while mixed has much lower PPL than n=8 (about 8.3 vs. 9.7). It also shows n=9 has about the same PPL as mixed (about 8.3) but higher memory usage (about 0.38 GB vs. 0.25 GB). The accompanying text also states the method maintains the n=8 memory footprint while improving perplexity.
The figure shows that for OPT-350M at 32K context length, both LoRA and LongLoRA are marked “OOM (>40),” and the text explicitly states that at 32K, LoRA and LongLoRA exceed 40 GB on OPT-350M.

The figure/caption states that Z_t is orthogonally projected to the tangent space to get \(\widehat Z_t\), normalized as \(\widetilde Z_t=\sqrt{mn}\widehat Z_t/\|\widehat Z_t\|_F\), and that two loss evaluations are performed at \(\Delta W_t\pm\epsilon\widetilde Z_t\) to obtain \(F_\pm\). It also states that \((F_+-F_-)/(2\epsilon)\) gives the directional derivative \(\widehat s_t\), yielding the zeroth-order Riemannian gradient \(\widehat G_t=\widehat s_t\widetilde Z_t\). Finally, the caption explicitly says truncated SVD retracts \(\Delta W_t-\eta\widehat G_t\) back to the rank-r manifold.

The cited evidence states that ZO fine-tuning suffers from slow convergence and a persistent performance gap to first-order methods, largely due to noisy estimates in high-dimensional and ill-conditioned parameter spaces. It also says existing methods remain limited by query efficiency, search-space quality, or update conditioning.

The cited evidence states that MeZO-SVRG uses periodic reference gradients to reduce variance and requires additional memory for stored parameters and gradients. It also states ENGINE’s analysis holds under stated assumptions and that exact subgrid correction eliminates curvature-mismatch bias in the local-linear limit.
The evidence explicitly states that raising the adapter rank from 4 to 8 improved accuracy by 1.3 points, from 71.2% to 72.5%, on Task T.
